title: How To Talk To Parents About Their Misbehaving Child ving-child/
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Linsin addresses a common teacher fear—discussing a child's misbehavior with parents—by naming the underlying anxieties: that parents will grow defensive, question competence, or make demands. He attributes these outcomes to how teachers typically phrase the conversation, and offers a script-like set of guidelines to keep meetings brief and productive. Recommendations include staying friendly and unguarded at the outset, sticking strictly to facts rather than opinions or rumor, avoiding an accusatory tone, stating plainly what behavior is not allowed and why, explaining the consequence already in motion, and keeping the whole exchange to about five minutes. He also notes that a classroom management packet sent home early in the year helps prevent parents from being blindsided later. The piece frames the goal as leaving parents informed and supportive rather than defensive, with responsibility for the misbehavior resting where it belongs—with the child.
points: Stay friendly and put parents at ease immediately—gravity and seriousness trigger defensiveness before you've said anything.
Inform, don't advise: stick to the facts of what happened and withhold opinions unless specifically asked.
State the rule and consequence plainly and confidently, without a 'so what are you going to do about it' undertone.
Send home a classroom management packet in week one so parent conversations about behavior are never a surprise.
Keep the conversation to about five minutes and end with a clear offer to follow up.
quotes: Their protective instinct kicks in, their emotions flare, and in an instant you find yourself backpedaling, apologizing, and explaining away your decisions and methods.

It’s a mistake to be grave or overly serious when speaking to parents, which causes them to put up a wall of defense before you even get to the purpose of your meeting. Put them at ease from the beginning.

A common mistake teachers make is that they affect an attitude of “so what are you gonna do about it” when speaking to parents. It’s almost as if they expect parents to make sure that it doesn’t happen again.
You can and should say, “This is the behavior I’m seeing, and any behavior, like this, that interferes with learning is not allowed in this classroom.” Don’t hold back in this regard.

Your conversation with parents should last no more than five minutes. As soon as you finish explaining how you’re handling the misbehavior, say, “Thanks for your support. Call me or come see me if you have any questions.
